THE GUY BUILDING GROK BOT AT SPACEX EXPLAINED EXACTLY HOW IT WORKS IN A FREE STANFORD LECTURE

Lee Robinson helped build Vercel and Cursor, and now he works on the team behind Grok Bot. At Stanford's CS146S he walked through the product, the infrastructure and the harness behind an agent that keeps working while you sleep.

Most AI tools sit and wait for your prompt. Grok Bot doesn't. It runs in the background, decides when it's time to act and finishes the job on its own, and this is the clearest look I've seen at how something like that is actually built.

Here's what's inside:

0:00 How we got here
3:38 What changed in the models
7:31 Inside an always-on agent
15:32 The harness
24:51 Context engineering
31:51 Where this is going

Start with the harness at 15:32. It's the part agent courses charge thousands for, and he explains it for free in under ten minutes.

You probably don't have 43 minutes right now, so don't let this one disappear from your feed.

Watch the lecture first, then read X's own guide to setting up Grok Bot below ↓ Together they give you the whole picture: how it works under the hood and how to put it to work for you.

I build my trading agents from the same pieces he walks through, so this one is going straight into my notes.

What's the first job you'd hand to an agent that never sleeps?

Save this before you lose it 🔖

note_tweet.text:
Your AI agent dies the second you close your laptop.

Lee Robinson, who works on Grok Bot, gave a Stanford lecture on the ones that don't.

Where the good parts are:

2:35 How we got here
From a tool loop in a terminal to an agent that wakes up without you.

6:13 What changed in the models
The shifts that made always-on possible at all.

10:06 Inside an always-on agent
The surprise: it sleeps almost all the time. Off after 2 idle minutes, back from saved state on the next message.

18:07 The harness
One tool for talking to you. Everything else stays private. Cheapest option gets tried first.

27:26 Context engineering
A cache miss is treated as a bug. Context is a budget, not a bucket.

34:26 Where this is going
Build the minimum around the model. Delete what it no longer needs.

The rule worth stealing sits outside any chapter title:

A risky action gets blocked.
You get an approval request.
No answer in 15 seconds, and it stays blocked.

Silence means no.

The breakdown attached applies that same default to coding agents: no evidence, no "done".
